metaDescription: Six compact cordless drills compared on head length, weight, torque and battery platform, for tight spaces, overhead work and long installs.
expertTake: The DeWalt DCD794B Atomic is the compact drill to buy if you already own 20V MAX batteries, and the Milwaukee M18 2606-21CT is the stronger choice if you are on M18. The Craftsman CMCD714D1 is the value pick with a 6.2 inch head. If your work never takes you into a cabinet or a stud bay, a full size drill is cheaper per unit of torque and you should skip this category.
introParagraphs: A compact drill trades a little torque for a lot of access. The shorter the head, the more places it fits, from between wall studs to the inside of a vanity. That is a real advantage, but the box seldom says how much power you give up to get it.
This guide explains how head length, weight and motor design shape a compact drill, when a subcompact 12V tool is enough and when it is not.

products.name: DeWalt DCD794B Atomic 20V MAX Brushless 1/2 Inch Drill Driver
products.description:
The DCD794B is the Atomic series drill, DeWalt's shortest and lightest brushless 20V MAX class. Its compact body fits where a standard drill will not, while the brushless motor keeps run time long for its size. A 1/2 inch chuck is retained, so bit range stays wide.

Compared with the DCD777D1 it is a more modern and more compact design, and it has the same battery platform. It is not as strong as the Milwaukee M18 2606-21CT, which publishes 500 in-lbs, but it is easier to hold overhead. For cabinet work, door hardware and small repairs it is excellent.

It is sold as a bare tool, so budget separately for batteries if you do not own them. Smaller packs make it very light, while larger packs add run time and weight. Spare batteries are the cheapest upgrade you can make to any of these.
products.bestFor: DeWalt platform owners who want the most compact drill.
pros: Atomic series body is short and light
Brushless motor keeps run time long
Half inch chuck holds large shanks
Shares batteries with 20V MAX tools
cons: Less torque than full size drills
Costs more than basic compact kits

products.name: Milwaukee M18 2606-21CT 1/2 Inch Compact Drill Driver Kit
products.description:
The Milwaukee 2606-21CT is an M18 compact drill with 500 in-lbs of torque and a speed range from 0 to 400 rpm in low and 0 to 1,800 rpm in high gear. That is more torque than any other compact on this page. REDLINK electronics protect the tool and battery from overload.

It uses a brushed 4-pole frameless motor, so it is not as efficient as the brushless DeWalt DCD794B. It is also heavier and bulkier than the Milwaukee M12 FUEL below. For drilling through studs, driving lag screws and running hole saws it is the compact to choose.

The kit arrives with a battery and charger, so it works at once. M18 is a deep platform, though the standard pack is large for what a compact tool deserves. Spare batteries are the cheapest upgrade you can make to any of these.
products.bestFor: Users who want compact size with real torque on M18.
pros: 500 in-lbs is high for a compact
REDLINK protects against overload
Wide speed range from 400 to 1,800 rpm
Kit includes battery and charger
cons: M18 battery is large for a compact tool

products.name: Milwaukee M12 FUEL 3/8 Inch Subcompact Drill Driver
products.description:
The M12 FUEL subcompact is the smallest brushless drill here, built for work where a 20V tool is simply too large. A 3/8 inch chuck suits screws and small drill bits, and the variable speed trigger gives precise control. It is the favorite of electricians and installers.

It cannot match the 500 in-lbs of the M18 2606-21CT, and the 3/8 inch chuck rules out large auger bits. In return it is lighter and smaller than every 20V drill, and the M12 battery is compact. For cabinet install and hardware it is a joy to use.

It is a bare tool, so buy an M12 battery separately. Keep the chuck clean, and use an impact driver on the same platform for large screws. Spare batteries are the cheapest upgrade you can make to any of these.
products.bestFor: Installers and electricians who want the smallest tool.
pros: Brushless motor in a subcompact body
Variable speed trigger gives fine control
M12 batteries are small and light
Ideal for cabinet and hardware work
cons: Bare tool needs a battery purchase

products.name: Craftsman V20 RP CMCD714D1 Brushless Compact Drill Driver Kit
products.description:
The Craftsman CMCD714D1 has a 6.2 inch head length, about 25 percent shorter than the maker's previous design, with a brushless motor and a 1/2 inch chuck. The kit includes a 2.0 Ah battery and charger. It claims to drill faster than a major competitor.

It is a direct rival to the DeWalt DCD777D1, usually at a lower price, with a smaller platform behind it. Compared with the DeWalt DCD794B it is similar in size, but it arrives as a complete kit. It will not match the 500 in-lbs of the M18.

It makes sense for homeowners who want compact access without a pro price. Keep the battery indoors and the chuck free of dust.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want a compact brushless kit at a lower price.
pros: 6.2 inch head fits tight spaces
Brushless motor in a low cost kit
Complete kit with battery and charger
1/2 inch chuck for wide bit range
cons: Smaller platform than DeWalt or Milwaukee

products.name: DeWalt DCD777D1 20V MAX Brushless Compact Drill Driver Kit
products.description:
The DCD777D1 is the compact brushless drill in a complete kit, with a 2.0 Ah battery and charger. It uses a two speed gearbox and a 1/2 inch chuck, so it covers drilling and driving. The lightweight body fits tight spaces, and the brushless motor extends run time.

Against the DCD794B it is slightly older and less compact, but it comes ready to use. Compared with the Craftsman CMCD714D1 it offers a deeper platform. The Milwaukee 2606-21CT beats it on torque.

It is the sensible entry to the 20V MAX family for someone who has no batteries. Add an impact driver later using the same pack.
products.bestFor: New DeWalt users who want a complete compact kit.
pros: Complete kit with battery and charger
Brushless motor and two speed gearbox
Light body fits tight spaces
Strong 20V MAX tool range
cons: Less compact than the Atomic DCD794B
Torque below the Milwaukee M18 compact

products.name: Dekopro 12V Compact Cordless Drill Set
products.description:
The Dekopro 12V drill weighs only 1.65 lb and is easy to run with one hand. Its top speed is 800 rpm, which is slow, and its 3/8 inch chuck is small. It has an LED light and is meant for wood and plastic.

Compared with the Milwaukee M12 FUEL it is far less capable, but it costs a fraction of the price. It suits assembly, crafts and small repairs where torque is not needed. It is not for hardwood or metal.

The set includes a case and accessories. Treat it as a light duty household tool and do not expect long term professional use.
products.bestFor: Light assembly and crafts on the smallest budget.
pros: Weighs only 1.65 lb for one hand use
LED light helps in dark corners
Low cost with accessories included
Easy for smaller hands to control
cons: Not meant for hardwood or metal

buyingCriteria.explanation: The distance from the back of the tool to the chuck decides where it fits. The Craftsman CMCD714D1 lists a 6.2 inch head, and the DeWalt Atomic series is similarly short. A drill over 8 inches long will not turn inside many cabinet carcasses. Measure the tightest space you work in before you shop.

Compact drills trade torque for size, and the gap is large. The Milwaukee M18 2606-21CT publishes 500 in-lbs, while light 12V models such as the Dekopro have far less. A compact tool that stalls in a stud forces you to fetch a bigger drill. Match torque to the toughest hole you expect.

Heat builds fast in a small housing, and brushless motors run cooler and use less power. The DeWalt DCD794B and DCD777D1, Craftsman CMCD714D1 and Milwaukee M12 FUEL are brushless. The M18 2606-21CT is brushed but makes up for it with torque. For frequent users the efficiency matters.

A smaller pack keeps the tool light, but run time falls. A 2.0 Ah pack is a good compromise for compact drills. Large 5 Ah packs add weight and defeat the purpose. Think of the pack as part of the tool's length and balance.

A 1/2 inch chuck accepts large shanks, while a 3/8 inch chuck stops at smaller bits. The DeWalt and Craftsman drills have 1/2 inch chucks, while the Milwaukee M12 FUEL and Dekopro use 3/8 inch. A compact body does not require a small chuck. Check the largest bit you plan to use.

A compact drill often becomes one of several tools you use. DeWalt 20V MAX and Milwaukee M18 or M12 have the broadest ranges. The Dekopro fits no other tool. Think about the saw, light or impact driver you will add next.

specDecoder.meaning: The measure from the chuck to the rear of the tool. A shorter head fits tighter spaces. The Craftsman CMCD714D1 lists 6.2 inches.
specDecoder.watchFor: Some makers measure to the back of the motor, not the battery, so total length may be longer.

specDecoder.meaning: The maximum twisting force. Compact drills range from low to 500 in-lbs on the Milwaukee M18 compact. More torque drives larger screws and bits.
specDecoder.watchFor: A compact with a low torque figure will stall in dense wood.

specDecoder.meaning: A class of tool smaller than compact, usually 12V. The Milwaukee M12 FUEL is a subcompact. It trades power for size and weight.
specDecoder.watchFor: Size labels are not standardized, so compare actual dimensions.

specDecoder.meaning: Spindle speed with nothing attached. The M18 compact reaches 1,800 rpm, while the Dekopro 12V reaches 800 rpm. Faster speeds drill small holes more cleanly.
A tool sold with no battery or charger. The DeWalt DCD794B and Milwaukee M12 FUEL are bare tools. They cost less if you own the platform.
specDecoder.watchFor: A bare tool costs more than a kit if you must also buy a battery.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and access
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared head lengths, such as 6.2 inches on the Craftsman CMCD714D1, and the overall feel of each body. The shortest tools ranked highest for access. Weight was weighed alongside length. Dimensions come from the maker's listing.

howWeEvaluated.title: Torque versus size
howWeEvaluated.description: We gave credit for torque in a small body, with the Milwaukee M18 2606-21CT at 500 in-lbs leading. Tools that gave up too much torque ranked lower. Real tasks like drilling studs set the bar. We did not penalize low torque in tools designed for light work.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and efficiency
howWeEvaluated.description: Brushless motors earned credit for run time and heat. We noted the brushed motor in the M18 compact. Efficiency matters in small housings. Heat in a small housing is the practical concern.

howWeEvaluated.title: Battery and kit
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted batteries and chargers in each kit. Bare tools suit platform owners. Kits suit newcomers. Charger speed and pack weight were noted.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The DCD794B leads for compact size, the M18 2606-21CT for torque and the M12 FUEL for smallest size. The Craftsman is the value pick and the Dekopro the lightest budget tool. Value per tool class shaped the order within tiers.

cards.label: Compact 18V to 20V
cards.text: More torque and a 1/2 inch chuck. The DeWalt DCD794B, DCD777D1, Craftsman CMCD714D1 and Milwaukee 2606-21CT fit here. They are heavier than subcompacts.

cards.label: Subcompact 12V
cards.text: Smaller and lighter, with a 3/8 inch chuck. The Milwaukee M12 FUEL and Dekopro 12V are in this group. They have limited torque.

howToChoose.note: Choose compact for general use and subcompact for installation work.

howToChoose.subheading: For Cabinet and Overhead Work Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A short head, low weight and a light. Weight matters overhead. A small battery keeps balance close to the hand.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The DeWalt DCD794B and Milwaukee M12 FUEL are best for tight overhead work. The Craftsman CMCD714D1 is a low cost option.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You install daily or want a platform. The Milwaukee M12 FUEL and DeWalt DCD794B repay the cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You work in tight spaces occasionally. The Craftsman CMCD714D1 or Dekopro 12V is enough.

maintenance.why: Compact housings trap heat. Dust makes it worse.
A loose chuck lets bits wobble. Tighten by hand.

maintenance.task: Charge batteries to half before storage
maintenance.why: Full or empty storage ages lithium cells. Keep them indoors.
Dull bits stall small motors. Replace worn ones.
Dust affects variable speed control. Use compressed air.

faq.q: Is a compact drill powerful enough for home use?
faq.a: Yes for most tasks. For studs and large holes pick a model with higher torque, like the Milwaukee M18 compact. Pilot holes, cabinet hardware and screws up to about 2.5 inches are well within reach of the compact class.

Compact fits tight spaces and weighs less. Full size gives more torque. Buy compact if you work in cabinets or overhead. Many tradespeople carry a compact for daily work and keep one full size drill for the rare large hole.
A class smaller than compact, usually 12V, such as the Milwaukee M12 FUEL. It is lighter and weaker. It is the right class for electricians, installers and anyone who works from a ladder.

faq.q: Do I need a kit or bare tool?
faq.a: A kit if you have no batteries. A bare tool if you already own the platform. Keep one platform where possible, since mixing brands means mixing chargers.

faq.q: Is brushless worth it in a compact drill?
faq.a: Yes for regular use. Heat is a concern in small bodies, and brushless motors run cooler. Small bodies have less surface area to shed heat, so efficiency translates into longer sessions.

faq.q: How do I measure head length?
faq.a: Measure from the chuck face to the back of the motor housing. Compare it with your tightest space. Remember to include the battery if it hangs below the handle, since that sets the real working footprint.
